name: Birthday-number effect
statement: People rate the numbers in their own birth date, the day and the month, as more likeable than other numbers.
meaning: The claim is about liking, not about use. Shown a run of numbers and asked how much each appeals to them, people put the day and the month of their own birth above the rest. Three separate claims travel together. The first is that preference, measured on a rating scale. The second is that the preference indexes self-esteem a respondent cannot manage, which turns the rating task into an instrument called the birthday number task. The third is that the preference steers decisions in the world, over where people live, what they pay and whom they marry. Each stands or falls on its own evidence. The letter version of the same argument is covered under the name-letter effect, entry 134, and the career and marriage disputes it feeds are covered under nominative determinism, entry 56. Bare preference among numerals, with no self-reference at all, is entry 272.

origin.note: The paper is "Implicit self-esteem in Japan: Name letters and birthday numbers", pages 736 to 742 of volume 23. It paired a letter-rating study with a number-rating study. Its question was why Japanese samples show no explicit self-enhancement. The full text was not obtained on 21 September 2026. Sage returned a Cloudflare bot challenge, which blocks automated access and is not the same thing as a paywall. The publisher-deposited abstract was read through Crossref. That abstract says Study 2 covered the numbers of the month and the day of the respondent's birthday. Simonsohn reports that the effect was much smaller, and not significant, for numbers below twelve. Nutt, DiMassimo and Hale describe the same study as covering month, day and year, which the abstract does not carry.

evidence: Bosson, Swann and Pennebaker ran the task on 84 University of Texas undergraduates, 40 men and 44 women, with one excluded. Participants rated every letter of the alphabet and the numbers 0 through 35 on a seven-point liking scale. A birthday-preference score subtracts the number's average popularity across all raters from the owner's own rating of it, so a person born on 19 November is scored on 19. The mean came to 0.73 scale points, SD 1.54, t(80) = 4.28. The initials version of the same task on the same people came to 0.93, SD 1.37, t(80) = 6.13. Nickell, Pederson and Rossow put 83 participants through a variety of dates and objects. They report a more positive evaluation of the birth month and the birth year than of other months and years, which they read as an extension of the mere ownership effect. Stieger and Krizan rated numbers in six countries, N = 657, and found the preference bending to local custom. Whether Christmas falls on 24 or 25 December moved the liking of those two numbers, and numerals used for good school grades were liked above numerals used for bad ones. Where grades are letters rather than numbers, no such effect appeared. The field claim starts elsewhere. Pelham, Mirenberg and Jones asked in their Study 6 whether people live in a city whose name begins with their birthday number. They used Social Security Death Index records, seven birth dates from 2 February to 8 August, and city names from Two to Eight. Of 485 people, 19.4% lived in a matching city against a chance value of 14.5%, chi-square(1) = 9.13, p = .003. Simonsohn restates the same table as a ratio of actual to expected frequency of 1.33.

examples.tag: The list of numerals to be rated
examples.text: Shown the numbers one to thirty-one and asked how much each appeals, a respondent rates the day of her own birth above its neighbours. Nothing in the task mentions birthdays, and she offers no reason for the gap.

examples.tag: The numbers written on a raffle line
examples.text: Asked to pick six numbers, a player puts down the day and the month of his birth first and finds the rest harder to settle. The claim is about which numerals feel agreeable, not about which of them win.

examples.tag: The door code that feels right
examples.text: Offered a choice of four-digit codes, a tenant prefers the one containing the month he was born in, and says only that it looks better than the others. A preference reported without a reason is what the effect is measured as.

replication.headline: The rating-task preference repeats in fresh samples; the archival claims built on it do not.
replication.detail: Nutt, DiMassimo and Hale ran the closest thing to a direct repeat of the original design. They gave 101 students at the University of North Georgia, 70 women and 31 men, the numbers 1 to 50 among distractor items on a four-point scale. Birthday numbers were rated above other numbers, F(1, 97) = 17.85, p < .001, partial eta squared .16. Month and day did not differ, F(1, 97) = 0.23, p = .64. The split between numbers 1 to 12 and 13 to 31 fell short at F(1, 97) = 3.68, p = .06, and its direction favoured the smaller numbers, against the original report. The authors attribute that reversal to fatigue, because they copied the original's fixed item order rather than counterbalancing it. Their self-esteem test came out flat, r(99) = -.02, p = .88. Women rated all numbers above men, F(1, 97) = 5.91, p = .017, but no interaction reached significance, Fs < 2.66, ps > .11. The archival side goes the other way. Simonsohn took the whole Social Security Death Index, N = 80.4 million, and asked whether the day of a person's birthday predicts living in a town named for that number. He found 967 matches against 954.5 expected, a ratio of 1.01, p = .46. He then used a New York voter registration file of 12.8 million people to test birthday numbers against address number, apartment number and street name. Not one of the 21 chi-square tests reached the 5% level and two reached the 10% level. The pooled ratios were .98 for address, 1.01 for apartment and 1.01 for street, with p values of .74, .73 and .50. He notes that his matching counts run 8 to 20 times larger than the originals and his samples 10,000 to 30,000 times larger. His reading is that the laboratory effect is real and too small to move a decision about where to live. His paper was read in the University of Pennsylvania repository copy, which is the accepted manuscript marked as forthcoming in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. Page numbers here come from Crossref.

study.cite: Nutt, C. G., DiMassimo, A. N., & Hale, R. G. (2024). Revisiting the birthday number effect, subjective preferences, and self-esteem in college students. Psi Chi Journal of Psychological Research, 29(2), 120-128.

limits: Number preferences only mean something against what people would have picked anyway, and every study here builds that baseline differently. Bosson subtracts each number's mean popularity across all raters, so common favourites are netted out. Nutt sets each person's birthday numbers against their own non-birthday numbers, which does not net them out. D'Hondt and colleagues compare ticket choices with a 13.33% probability under random drawing. Pelham derives expected city frequencies from the margins of a seven by seven table. A gap between two studies may therefore be a gap between two baselines. The measure is also weak where it is used as a measure. In Bosson's sample the birthday task correlated -.10, .17, .00 and .00 with four explicit self-esteem scales, none of them reliable, and .23 with the initials task run on the same people. Its retest correlation over a mean of 31.23 days was .53, against .80 for the Rosenberg scale. Falk, Heine, Takemura, Zhang and Hsu gave the birthday number task with the numbers 1 to 40 to Euro-Canadians, Asian-Canadians and Japanese, 107, 187 and 112 people. Their second study recruited 623 Americans on Mechanical Turk, of whom 582 passed an attention check and were analysed. Among Asian-Canadians the task correlated with explicit self-esteem at a mean of -.15, range -.22 to -.09, and the authors conclude that implicit self-esteem measures are not valid for individual or cross-cultural comparison. Blanton and Jaccard's argument about arbitrary metrics is relevant to what such a score could mean, though their two worked cases are the Implicit Association Test and clinical intervention research, not number preference. The largest test of the preference is behavioural. D'Hondt, Roger, Hoffmann and Plotkina recruited 506 Belgians for an online survey and analysed 498 after excluding incomplete responses. On the first of two lotto tickets, 59.44% selected their birth day and 39.76% their birth month, against 13.33% under random choice. Women selected their birth day more often than men, 63.45% against 55.77%, but that gap only reaches the 10% level, t(496) = -1.74, p = .0817. The gender gap is firmer on the self-declared measure, 5.16 against 4.54, t(495.64) = -3.56, p = .0004, and in a logit model where being a woman carries an odds ratio of 1.647. On the second ticket, filled in straight after the first, birth-day selection fell to 14%, which does not differ from the random-choice value, and the gender term lost significance. Participants took 31.88 seconds on the first ticket and 19.76 on the second. The authors read birthday-number play as deliberative rather than automatic, since those who played their birthday numbers took about 8 seconds longer, t(496) = -2.67, p = .0078. That reverses what Koole and colleagues had reported. Their copy was read as the publisher-typeset version in the UCLouvain DIAL repository, with the page range taken from Crossref. No preregistered test of the basic rating preference was located on 21 September 2026 in Crossref, OpenAlex, Unpaywall, Semantic Scholar, PubMed, ERIC or open web search. The nearest thing to a large pooled analysis is Pietschnig and colleagues on the initial preference task, 105 samples and 17,777 people, of which only five used a measure compounding birthday-number liking with the letter task. Four items could not be read. Kitayama and Karasawa, Nickell and colleagues, and Coulter and Grewal sit behind a Cloudflare bot challenge at Sage; Jones, Pelham, Mirenberg and Hetts behind one at Elsevier; Pelham and Carvallo behind one at Taylor and Francis; and Blanton and Jaccard behind an automated-access block at the American Psychological Association. In none of those cases was a paywall actually reached. Keller and Gierl is a real paywall, a Springer chapter offered for sale at $39.99.
misreadings: Simonsohn is read as having overturned the effect. He did not test it. He calls the laboratory evidence for implicit egotism abundant and convincing, and says the effect may act where a chooser is close to indifferent, which is not how a town or a spouse is chosen. Evidence that people like their own numbers is not evidence for the life-outcome claims built on top, and those claims have been attacked on confounding grounds rather than on the liking. The instrument and the phenomenon are also collapsed. Failures of the birthday number task as a self-esteem measure say nothing about whether people like their own numbers, and the liking says nothing about what the task measures. The scoring rule is narrower than the name suggests. Bosson's version scores the day alone, the abstract of Kitayama and Karasawa covers month and day, and Nickell's covers month and year, so three studies under one heading count three different things. A marginal result should not be read flat either. The lotto gender gap is significant at the 10% level on ticket choice and at the 0.1% level on the self-report. The commercial extension is a claim of its own. Coulter and Grewal report that prices whose cents digits match a buyer's birth date raise liking and purchase intention, to the point of a higher-priced product beating a cheaper one. Their paper, read at its publisher abstract, is the source for that claim rather than any of the rating studies.
